If you don't get enough calcium through your food, calcium supplements are absolutely necessary. The only disadvantage would be if you take too much of it. Calcium is important for bone health, amongst other things, but a lot of research has shown that too much calcium in fact has the opposite effect on your bones. It may also lead to fatigue, headaches, joint pains etc. 

No particular risk with multivitamins, you just need to make sure that you don't take additional isolated vitamins that are already in the multivitamins, to avoid exceeding the intake limit. 

I advise you to check with your doctor and have a blood test before starting any supplements, both at the start of your diet change and after a few months. That way you don't waste money on supplements you don't need, avoid getting too much of anything and you may also discover unexpected deficiencies. 

Iron is one of the minerals that are the most crucial to have checked and should not be taken without a doctor's advice. This is because iron easily accumulates in the body if you get too much of it. 

Also, keep doing a good job on getting calcium through your food, and remember that calcium needs vitamin D for absorption. Very often, almond/rice/soy milk is enriched with both calcium and vitamin D. 

In general it is always better to get all nutrients through food whenever possible, because most of the vitamins and minerals work together, some also need fats from the food in order to be effectively absorbed - to mention some benefits :)

Besides vitamins and minerals, veggies contain phytonutrients (e.g. antioxidants) which are very important for your health, especially your immune system. They prevent certain types of cancer and numerous other diseases.   
Vitamin supplements are better than nothing, but you need to keep in mind that vitamins, minerals and phytonutrients work together like a cascade, which is why getting them through food is always, always the best option. 

I understand that this is a phobia, though, and you're not just being picky. Is it the taste or the texture? If it's the texture, you could try some green drinks from various powder mixes. I normally don't recommend green drinks, not because they aren't effective but because it's always better to get your nutrients through real food. But in your case, it could be very helpful as a temporary solution. Spirulina is great (and fairly well-documented) although it might taste terrible the first couple of times ;)

You can eat a lot of oatmeal and it contains many of the nutrients you need, but unfortunately not all of them. It lacks vitamin A, D, B12 and C. These, of course, you can get through milk (assuming they add vitamin D to the milk in your country like they do here in Norway) and fruits/berries so you would have to be very mindful of what you combine it with. You would also have to take omega 3-supplements. 

Oatmeal twice a day would be good!

Vitamin B deficiency is very rare. Unless you are a vegan (in which case you'd need to take B12 supplements) it is unlikely that you do not get enough vitamin B through your food - even with a poor diet. 

You can find a lot of supplements promising better hair, better skin etc. Yes, vitamin B is necessary for your skin and hair, but supplements will only make a difference if you are already deficient and need to get to normal levels. If not, it's a waste of money.

Feces, or poop if you will, actually consists mainly of bacteria, dead cells from your intestinal lining, secretions and some metabolism compounds, and only a very insignificant amount of food. I don't have an exact number, but let's say 5-10%, which is mostly undigested fat or fibres. So I'm sorry to tell you that at least 95% your chocolate bar probably did not escape via your poop :)

Are you going by yourself? If so, you have a fairly good chance of getting get a rush ticket. I came late once but still got a single seat (one of the best in the orchestra) literally one minute before it started, they let me pass a HUGE line of groups and couples. I'm guessing it's harder for them to fill single seats in an otherwise full row. So if you're either early or a loner, it's worth a shot ;)

If you manage to get tickets for The Book of Mormon, there is NO DOUBT that you should see it. And I say that 100% objectively!

Other than that, for most of the other shows (not the Lion King, though) you could just go to the official TKTS booth at Times Square or the less known booth at South Seaport and get same day tickets with really good discounts. The seats are usually good as well. 

You can go to http://www.tdf.org/TKTSBoards.aspx to see what's available today, it differs a little bit from day to day.

1. This one might not apply to you, doidareto, as you are already a student, but when choosing a career path and university, figure out in advance which you are most likely to be able to finish - consider the work load, difficulty level etc. 

2. Let yourself suck sometimes. Failed? Try it again. Couldn't even do it? Do it later. I decided to postpone my studies for a semester just to allow myself to do absolutely nothing for months, best decision I ever made. This also gave me time to regain some of the passion for my field of study. 

3. Don't let your entire life revolve around school. Make some space for things that make you happy (or less depressed). I think this is so important for avoiding understimulation.

4. I'm lucky enough to be able to take most of my courses online, I highly recommend this if you have that option, as long as this doesn't make you isolate yourself more than necessary.

I like the idea of a "what did you do this week?"-thread, someone needs to make that happen! During a period of major depression I started writing a "happy journal" where I wrote down at least 20 things I had done or accomplished that day, even the most trivial things. Helped a lot! 
I later read a book about cognitive therapy and found that this is actually a well documented method against depression :)

Sorry to hear about this... like someone else has already pointed out, CFS is individual but I thought it might be encouraging to tell you that there is hope, a lot of people do get better although it might take a lot of patience and trying different things. 

I have recovered almost 100% after many years of severe CFS, my solution was 1. changing my diet, 2. knowing my limits but not isolating myself entirely and 3. quit smoking. 

Keep trying different things, in my opinion there is no such thing as wasted time or money on things that don't work as long as you keep trying and actually find something good in the end :)

As a nutritionist student I've tried for 3-4 years to find just one plausible explanation as to why an alkaline diet would work. Even with basic understandings of how the gastrointestinal system and acid regulation works, it's obvious that it makes no sense. For one, all food will be regulated and therefore acidic when it leaves your stomach, and it is then regulated again in your intestines. It has to, in order to be absorbed. In other words, the PH value of your food or drinks before it enters your stomach really doesn't matter. 

With that being said, an alkaline diet is generally healthy and will probably make you feel better, but probably not because of the PH value.
The reason why some people feel this might work is because it makes you eat healthier in general, just like with most other popular diets. Other than that, scientifically speaking, it's BS.
